explanations.explanation: Prophecy it is, baker. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says to pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, “…especially the gift of prophecy.” (1 Corinthians 14:1) Out of the whole tray, he points at one cookie and says, 'That one.'

Good guess, but healing isn't the one Paul names here. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says to eagerly desire spiritual gifts, “…especially the gift of prophecy.” (1 Corinthians 14:1) He circles prophecy right in the same breath as love.

I get why faith feels like a safe pick, friend. But Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, names a different gift in this verse. He says to eagerly desire spiritual gifts, “…especially the gift of prophecy.” (1 Corinthians 14:1)

Right, friend. The one who speaks in a tongue speaks to God, but the one who prophesies speaks to men. Paul says it's for their edification, encouragement and comfort (1 Corinthians 14:3). Three good things in one sentence, and none of them are small.

Other way around, baker. Paul says the one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God (1 Corinthians 14:2). Then he says that “…he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort.” (1 Corinthians 14:3) So prophecy is the one aimed at people.

Himself, yes. Paul says the one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). One gift builds up the speaker, and the other builds up the whole room. Paul is just laying them side by side.

Angels are nice company in a bakery, but they're not in this verse. Paul says the one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself. The one who prophesies edifies the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). The two gifts are being compared by who gets built up.

Elders don't show up in this verse, friend. Paul says the one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, while the one who prophesies edifies the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). The blank is the speaker, and the church is the other half of the comparison.

That's the exception. Paul says the one who prophesies is greater, “…unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.” (1 Corinthians 14:5) When the tongue gets interpreted, the church can understand it too. Everyone gets a bite.

Praying is a fine thing, baker, but it's not the exception Paul gives. He says the one who prophesies is greater, “…unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.” (1 Corinthians 14:5) Interpreting is what changes the picture.

explanations.answer: Unless the whole church joins in
explanations.explanation: A crowd doesn't change it, friend. Even a full room can't understand a tongue by itself. Paul says the one who prophesies is greater, “…unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.” (1 Corinthians 14:5) Interpreting is the exception.

Distinct, that's the word. Paul asks how anyone will recognize the tune a flute or harp is playing “…unless the notes are distinct?” (1 Corinthians 14:7) If every note melts into the next, you're not hearing a song, you're hearing a mystery. Clear notes let the tune come through.

Loud is tempting, and I'm a loud guy myself, friend. But Paul never says the notes need to be loud. He asks how anyone will recognize the tune “…unless the notes are distinct?” (1 Corinthians 14:7) You can blast a flute all day, and if the notes are mushy, nobody knows the song.

High notes are fun, but that's not Paul's point. He says no one will recognize the tune of the flute or harp “…unless the notes are distinct.” (1 Corinthians 14:7) Low, high or in between, the tune only comes through when each note is clear.
Careful, baker, Paul says the opposite. He asks, “…if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8) A muffled call doesn't get anybody ready. A clear one does.

Right, it's False. Paul asks, “…if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8) A mumbled trumpet leaves everyone standing around asking each other what that was. A clear call gets people moving.

explanations.answer: Their words must be understood to help
explanations.explanation: That's his point. Paul says, “Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.” (1 Corinthians 14:9) The flute and the trumpet were his examples. Words that nobody can understand don't help the people listening.

The flute, harp and trumpet make it sound that way, baker. But the music is just the example. Paul's point is, “Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying?” (1 Corinthians 14:9) It's about being understood, not about adding instruments.

Volume isn't the problem here, friend. A muffled trumpet is unclear, and unclear is what Paul worries about. He says, “Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.” (1 Corinthians 14:9) Understandable beats louder.

Foreigner, yes. Paul says, “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” (1 Corinthians 14:11) Two people in the same room, and neither one can follow the other. That's what an unexplained language does.

Servant is a good word, but it isn't in this verse. Paul says, “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” (1 Corinthians 14:11) The word is foreigner, because neither one understands the other.

Paul does call the Corinthians brothers elsewhere in this chapter (1 Corinthians 14:6), friend. But in this verse he says, “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” (1 Corinthians 14:11) Not understanding the language is what makes them foreigners to each other.

explanations.answer: The gifts that build up the church
explanations.explanation: That's the target, baker. Paul says, “Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.” (1 Corinthians 14:12) The Corinthians were already eager. Paul just points that eagerness at building up the church.

Impressing people isn't what Paul asks for. He says, “Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.” (1 Corinthians 14:12) The goal is building up the church, not making a show for outsiders.

explanations.answer: The gifts that are hardest to get
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about how hard a gift is to get, friend. He says, “Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.” (1 Corinthians 14:12) The measure is whether it builds up the church.

explanations.answer: Pray with his spirit and his mind
explanations.explanation: Both, baker. Paul says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) He doesn't pick one or the other, he brings the whole self to prayer.

explanations.answer: Pray only with his mind from now on
explanations.explanation: Close, but Paul keeps both. He says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) The word is also, friend. His mind joins in, and his spirit doesn't leave.

Paul isn't quitting tongues, friend. He says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) A few verses later he thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them (1 Corinthians 14:18).
Not quite, baker. Paul says, “I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) His mind comes along for the song too. It stays in the choir.
Right, it's False. Paul says, “I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) Spirit and mind sing together. Nobody gets left in the green room.

Amen, that's it. Paul says, “…if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say ‘Amen’ to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Corinthians 14:16) Saying Amen means you're agreeing with what was said, and you can't agree with something you can't follow.

Hosanna is a great word, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Paul asks how the uninstructed person can say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, “…since he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Corinthians 14:16) Amen is the word the person can't say, because he can't follow the blessing.

Maranatha is a fun word to say, baker, but it's not what Paul writes here. He asks how the uninstructed person can say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, “…since he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Corinthians 14:16) Amen is the missing word.

True, and I love it. Paul says, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” (1 Corinthians 14:18) So when he says prophecy comes first in church, it's not because he's never done tongues. He has, more than anybody in the room.

I can see why it sounds that way, baker. But Paul says, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” (1 Corinthians 14:18) Tongues are something he has, and he thanks God for it. He just puts clear words first when the church is together.

explanations.answer: Five clear words that instruct others
explanations.explanation: Five clear words, yes. Paul says, “…in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.” (1 Corinthians 14:19) That math is hard to argue with. Five words that land are worth more than ten thousand that don't.

Ten beautiful words sound lovely, friend, but they're not in the verse. Paul says, “…in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.” (1 Corinthians 14:19) The word that matters is coherent, and the goal is instructing others.

Silence isn't what Paul has in mind. He says, “…in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.” (1 Corinthians 14:19) He wants spoken words that people can follow and learn from.
Evil, yes. Paul says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 14:20) Be as green as a newborn when it comes to evil. When it comes to thinking, grow up.

Prayer is a good one to grow in, so Paul doesn't tell them to be infants there. He says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 14:20) The blank is evil, and the maturity belongs in their thinking.
Giving doesn't come up in this verse, baker. Paul says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 14:20) Be infants about evil, and mature in how you think.

Close, baker, but Paul flips it. He says, “Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers.” (1 Corinthians 14:22) So tongues are a sign for unbelievers, and prophecy, he says, is for believers. Easy to swap them in your head, so don't sweat it.

Right, it's False. Paul says, “Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers.” (1 Corinthians 14:22) The card had half the sentence turned around, and you caught it.

explanations.answer: That you are out of your minds
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. If the whole church speaks in tongues and some uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, “…will they not say that you are out of your minds?” (1 Corinthians 14:23) A visitor who can't understand a word of it isn't going to know what to make of the room.

explanations.answer: That you are just showing off
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, friend, but Paul words it differently. He asks, “…will they not say that you are out of your minds?” (1 Corinthians 14:23) The visitors hear something they can't make sense of, so they wonder about the people.

explanations.answer: That you are a holy people
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice review, baker, but it's not what Paul says. He asks, “…will they not say that you are out of your minds?” (1 Corinthians 14:23) A visitor who understands nothing isn't going to leave a glowing review.

explanations.answer: He will fall facedown and worship God
explanations.explanation: Yes, and that's quite a turnaround. Paul says, “So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, ‘God is truly among you!’” (1 Corinthians 14:25) The secrets of his heart are made known, and he ends up on his face worshiping.

explanations.answer: He will walk out without a word
explanations.explanation: Not this visitor, baker. Paul says the secrets of his heart will be made known, “So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, ‘God is truly among you!’” (1 Corinthians 14:25) He doesn't slip out the back. He worships.

explanations.answer: He will ask someone to interpret
explanations.explanation: Interpreting belongs to the tongues scene, friend. Here everyone is prophesying, and the visitor understands. Paul says, “So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, ‘God is truly among you!’” (1 Corinthians 14:25)
